title: Final letters
hook: five letters change shape at the end of a word

segments.voice: Yesterday, tav, the last letter, and emet spanning the whole alef-bet. Your line was truth from alef to tav. Did the true sentence get said? Today, the end of a week, and the letters that change at the end. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

Melech. King. Three letters: mem, lamed, kaf. At the start of a word, kaf is a rounded shape that sits on the line, like the cupped palm from a few days back. But at the end of melech it does something else. It straightens, and its tail drops down below the line, as if the word were stepping off a curb. Same letter, same sound, new shape. And kaf isn't alone. Mem, which you met in mayim, does it too, and so do nun, peh and tzadi. The Talmud groups the five under one made-up word, mantzepach, built from the letters themselves. Today's word is what those endings are called.
screen: `MELECH: A KAF AT THE END.` → `SAME SOUND, NEW SHAPE.` → `MANTZEPACH: THE FIVE.`

segments.voice: Sofit. It means final, from sof, end. A mem sofit is a final mem. Four things to know. First, the shapes. Final mem closes into a box. The other four stretch out: final kaf, nun, peh and tzadi drop a long tail down below the line, as if the word were leaning into the space after it. Second, the seers. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the final forms were spoken by the tzofim, the watchmen or seers. Then it raises a puzzle: if the Torah was given with them, how could later people have introduced them? Its answer is that they were known, then forgotten, then restored. The rabbis cared enough about the shape of an ending to argue about where it came from. Third, the bent and the straight. On that same page, the Talmud reads the nun and the tzadi as pairs. A bent nun and a straight nun: a person who is faithful when bent low will be faithful when standing straight. A bent tzadi and a straight tzadi: the same for the righteous. Remember the nun that fell in Ashrei, and the tzadi of Noah in his generations. Here they get a second shape, standing upright at the end. Fourth, the week. It began with peh, the mouth, and Moses slow of speech. Then tzadi, the righteous one. Kuf, holy. Resh, the head of the year. Shin on the doorpost. Tav, the seal of truth. And now the endings. Two of this week's letters, peh and tzadi, have a final form of their own. In Hebrew, how a word ends is visible on the page. The last letter stands differently.
screen: `SOFIT: FINAL, FROM SOF, END.` · `A CLOSED BOX AND FOUR LONG TAILS.` · `THE SEERS SPOKE THEM, THE TALMUD SAYS.` · `BENT NOW, STRAIGHT AT THE END.` · then, large: `FIVE ENDINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one final letter. If you have a pen and paper, take them. If not, use a fingertip on your palm. Settle, and breathe. Draw a final nun: one straight stroke, from the top down, past where the line would be. Draw it slowly, and let the stroke go all the way down without hurrying. Then think of one thing in your life that's ending this week. A project, a season, a habit, a hard stretch. Ask how you'd like it to end: closed and complete, like a final mem, or upright and reaching on, like that nun. Draw the shape of that ending. If you pray, you can bring it in. The bell holds the time.
Sofit. Final: the end form of five letters, kaf, mem, nun, peh and tzadi. Today's word.
Your line: five endings. Today, finish one small thing on purpose, and give its last step the care you'd give its first. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Hebrew writes five letters, kaf, mem, nun, peh and tzadi, in a final form (sofit) at the end of a word; the Talmud groups them under the made-up word mantzepach and discusses them in Shabbat 104a.

pairs: a word to remember the five

myth: every Hebrew letter has a final form
only five: kaf, mem, nun, peh and tzadi.
final mem is closed, while the other four final forms stretch below the line
mem closes into a box; the others drop a long tail.
the Talmud says the final forms were spoken by the seers
then asks how that fits the Torah, and answers: known, forgotten, restored.

fork.setup: you're writing melech, king, in Hebrew. you reach the last letter, a kaf. which shape do you write?
options: the rounded kaf, the same as at the start of a word.
the final kaf, with its tail dropping below the line.
fork.reveal: at the end of a word, kaf straightens and drops its tail below the line: kaf sofit.

original.note: Hebrew: final — the end form of a letter, from sof, end.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hebrew just has some extra letters.
what it means: five letters take a final shape, sofit, at the end of a word — same sound, new form.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 104a — mantzepach spoken by the seers, forgotten and restored; bent and straight nun and tzadi read as the faithful and the righteous.

notes: Shabbat 104a paraphrased: mantzepach 'tzofim amrum' (the seers said them), the bent/straight nun and tzadi readings. The 'known, forgotten, restored' answer is in Shabbat 104a and Megillah 2b–3a; confirm the summary.
'Children learning Hebrew often memorize the five with mantzepach': general classroom practice; confirm or soften.
Shapes: final mem closed; final kaf, nun, peh and tzadi descend below the line. Confirm the description of final peh and tzadi.
Week-end look-back names the week's letters peh through sofit (days 1345–1351) from the index.
Sof/sofit given as end/final: standard vocabulary, not a contested etymology.
